2.text: The first shoals pass northward in May with the drifting ice. The later ones

3.text: begin to leave their winter places in Holy Cross Bay about a month after the

4.text: first migration, and go northwards all along the shore. At the end of June,

5.text: when returning from Indian Point to the mouth of the Anadyr, we met in one

6.text: day, near the village ᴇˊnmɪlɪn, a great many of these shoals, containing perhaps

7.text: more than a thousand animals. Their course lay a few miles from the shore;

8.text: and the natives everywhere would open on them a most wanton shooting, killing

9.text: a few, and wounding many more. Next day we saw on the shore in different

10.text: places three large walrus-carcasses. The animals had evidently died from wounds,

11.text: and were carried by the tide to the shore. One was already in a quite putrid state.

12.text: On the whole, at least half of the wounded sea-animals — seals, walruses,

13.text: and white whales — escape the hunter, and are afterwards drifted ashore in

14.text: a putrid state. Any animal of this kind that is found by the people is used

15.text: for dog-food, and the blubber is tried out for lamp-oil, but of course the greater

16.text: number are wasted. Several times I saw a man who was shooting from the

17.text: shore use about three dozen cartridges in three hours. Although nearly every

18.text: shot was well aimed, he would secure but a single seal. Of the others, two or

19.text: three would occasionally be found afterwards by other people, twenty or twenty-

20.text: five miles off, but without benefit to the hunter.

21.text: In the middle of September the walrus start on the return journey. The

22.text: natives assert that at this time the walrus are most easily killed, since they

23.text: are quite unmindful of the hunter’s presence until the shooting begins. Several

24.text: boats join in the hunt in order to cut off the retreat of the animals. A peculiar

25.text: kind of splasher (Fig. 40), made of seal-skin and about three feet long and

26.text: four inches wide, is used to frighten the animals. Every time the walrus dive,

27.text: several splashers from various boats are struck against the water, making a

28.text: sharp sound, similar to the report of a gun. The walrus are so much frightened

29.text: that they hasten to come out again, and are shot. After diving and emerging

30.text: a few times, they become quite confused, and cannot discern which sounds are

31.text: connected with the real danger. The wounded walrus are despatched by

32.text: means of a long lance with an iron point (Fig. 41).
